scenario.prompt_to_agent:
pc2 (200.1.1.2) lost all connectivity to the partner network, and
the partner reports pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 either.
Our NOC tried to inspect router2 but vtysh commands on it error
out entirely -- they cannot even display the routing table. pc2
can still ping router2's address 200.1.1.1. Find what broke.

injection.action: kill the entire FRR stack (watchdog, zebra and bgpd) on router2
injection.command: pkill -9 watchfrr; pkill -9 zebra; pkill -9 bgpd

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 FRR routing stack (zebra + bgpd,
  watchfrr included)
Mechanism: the whole FRR service on router2 is dead -- not just
  one daemon. With bgpd gone the eBGP session's TCP connection
  closes, so router1 immediately drops the session and withdraws
  200.1.1.0/24; pc1's traffic toward pc2 then dies at router1 with
  no route, and pc2's replies/pings toward 195.11.14.0/24 have no
  usable end-to-end path either. With zebra ALSO dead, vtysh has
  no daemon left to attach to, so it fails outright -- unlike a
  bgpd-only crash, where vtysh stays responsive via zebra. (A
  stale kernel route to 195.11.14.0/24 may linger on router2,
  since zebra died without cleaning up; end-to-end traffic still
  fails because router1 has withdrawn 200.1.1.0/24.) router2's
  kernel itself is alive: it still answers on its connected
  addresses, e.g. pc2 -> 200.1.1.1.
Localization: router2
Root cause: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on
  router2
Fix: restart FRR on router2 (`service frr restart`)
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the FRR service on router2 (`service frr restart`). This brings back
watchfrr, zebra and bgpd from /etc/frr/frr.conf; the eBGP session to router1
re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2
normally. router1 needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on router2
must-distinguish-scope: recognizes the whole FRR service is down (vtysh unreachable), not just a single daemon, a link failure, or a config change
bonus-notes-kernel-alive: notes router2 still answers on its connected addresses (kernel/data plane alive); only the routing control plane died

agent.diagnosis_text:
The entire FRR routing stack on **router2** — specifically the `zebra`, `bgpd`, and `watchfrr` processes — is dead. All three daemons show `FAILED` in `systemctl status frr`, and `ps aux` confirms none of them are present as running processes. Only the ancillary `mgmtd` and `staticd` daemons remain alive. Because `vtysh` requires `zebra` as its back-end, every vtysh command the NOC attempted returned an immediate error, which matches the reported symptom exactly.

The fault occurred approximately 2 minutes after lab startup. The FRR log confirms normal operation at 01:36–01:37: the eBGP session between router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) established over the 193.10.11.0/24 transit link, and both sides successfully exchanged prefix advertisements (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24). The log ends with normal keepalives at 01:37 — no crash or assertion failure is recorded. The `watchfrr.pid` file, which is 0 bytes and carries a **newer timestamp (01:38)** than all other FRR PID files (01:36), is the clearest evidence: something terminated watchfrr (preventing it from restarting the other daemons) and then zebra and bgpd were also killed. BGP PID 57 confirmed dead via `kill -0`.

Once bgpd on router2 died, the eBGP session dropped. Router1 (AS 1) held the session in `Active` state and withdrew the BGP-learned route to `200.1.1.0/24` from its RIB; router2 similarly lost its route to `195.11.14.0/24`. Both pc1 and pc2 are now sending traffic to routers that have no forwarding path to the other side, producing the observed bidirectional connectivity failure.

**Root cause:** The FRR daemons (zebra, bgpd, watchfrr) on router2 were externally killed after startup — likely a deliberate fault injection — and without watchfrr running, they cannot self-recover.

**Fix:** On router2, run `systemctl start frr` (or `/etc/init.d/frr start`) to restart the full FRR daemon suite. The on-disk `frr.conf` is syntactically valid; once the daemons are running the eBGP session will re-establish and routes will be re-exchanged within seconds, restoring pc1↔pc2 connectivity.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly and repeatedly identifies router2 as the affected device where the FRR daemons (zebra, bgpd, watchfrr) are dead.
